messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 59
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Professor
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 54

The patient, a 59-year-old African man, a professor of comparative literature, sits in the chair with a stillness that feels deliberate, as if he is holding himself together against a strong wind. He speaks in a low, measured voice, each word chosen with the precision he uses in his lectures. He is single, lives alone in a small apartment crowded with books, and has not set foot on campus in three weeks.

His story begins not with a bang, but with a phone call. Eight months ago, on a Tuesday afternoon, his phone buzzed in his pocket while he was in the middle of a seminar on postcolonial narrative. He ignored it. When he checked his messages afterward, he had a voicemail from his younger sister, Amara, who still lived in their home country. Her voice was not her own. It was thin, frayed. She said, "The men came. They took our brother. They took Kofi."

Kofi, his eldest nephew, a bright, gentle young man who had just finished his engineering degree. The men were from a local militia. They accused him of being a government informant, a completely baseless charge. For three days, the patient lived in a state of frantic, impotent action. He called every number he had, wired money for a ransom that was never collected, and stared at his phone until his eyes burned. On the third day, Amara called again. Kofi’s body had been found in a ditch. He had been tortured. He was twenty-four years old.

The patient did not cry. He did not scream. He sat in his office, in the dark, and felt a cold, sharp crack run through the center of his chest. He finished the semester. He graded papers, attended faculty meetings, and delivered lectures on the structure of grief in African literature. He was, to all appearances, a functioning man.

But the world has since become a hostile, unpredictable place. He can no longer sit in a lecture hall. The moment he stands at the podium, the soft hum of the projector and the shuffling of students’ notebooks become a wall of noise. His peripheral vision sharpens to a painful clarity. He sees every exit, every shadow in the corner, the way the light falls on a student’s face. His heart hammers against his ribs, and his palms become slick with sweat. He feels a suffocating pressure in his throat, as if the air has turned to sand. He has had to excuse himself from three classes this semester, leaving his students bewildered and concerned.

At home, the silence is worse. He cannot sleep. He lies in bed, his body rigid, listening to the creaks of the old building. Every sound is a prelude to a door being kicked in. He has removed all the photographs of his family from the walls. He cannot look at Kofi’s face without seeing the image his mind has created: Kofi, tied to a chair, alone and terrified. The image is not a memory; he was not there. But it is more real to him than any lecture he has ever given. It is a loop, playing behind his eyelids.

He has stopped answering his sister’s calls. Her voice is a direct line to that Tuesday afternoon. He knows she is suffering, but he cannot carry her pain and his own. He feels a profound, corrosive guilt. He was the one who paid for Kofi’s education. He was the one who encouraged him to stay in the country, to build a future. "I sent him to his death," he says, his voice finally breaking for a fraction of a second before he regains his composure. "I told him to be brave. And he was. And it killed him."

He now spends his days in his apartment, reading the same page of a book over and over, unable to absorb a single word. He is a professor who cannot teach, an elder who cannot comfort his family, a man who is being slowly hollowed out by a story that has no ending. He is not here for a diagnosis. He is here because he does not know what else to do. He is simply waiting for the weight of the world to become too heavy to bear.
